title: One-Step Generation via Riemannian Wasserstein Gradient Flows

paper.title: One-Step Generation via Riemannian Wasserstein Gradient Flows
paper.abstract: Abstract Recently, Drifting Models and Wasserstein Gradient Flows have attracted substantial attention because they move iterative distributional refinement to training and amortize it into a generator, enabling fast inference. However, existing formulations have been developed largely for continuous Euclidean domains, such as image spaces, where particles admit unconstrained additive updates. On constrained spaces, these updates can leave the valid domain or ignore its geometry, making them unsuitable targets for training. Recent work has adapted updates to these spaces, but has focused on particular fields or offered limited empirical comparison. We derive and compare several geometry-aware fields within a common training framework for one-step generators. We test the method on data with different structures and obtain competitive one-step results in each setting. The best-performing field varies by task, showing why the choice of objective matters in practice.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-based generators achieve strong sample quality by gradually transporting a simple reference distribution toward the data distribution ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) . This transport is often realized through many sequential updates, making inference expensive. Drifting Models offer a complementary strategy: they update the model distribution iteratively during training and amortize the resulting moves into a generator that can be evaluated directly at inference time ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . Recent works connect such updates to Wasserstein gradient flows (WGFs), making it possible to derive the drift from an explicit objective ( Gretton et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Most such formulations, however, rely on Euclidean velocities and additive updates. Many data types and representations live naturally on curved or constrained spaces, where Euclidean updates need not follow the intrinsic geometry or even remain in the state space. Classical WGF theory extends beyond Euclidean spaces ( Ambrosio et al., 2005 ; Erbar, 2010 ) , and recent generative and drifting methods construct dynamics on Riemannian manifolds ( Chen and Lipman, 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) . However, they typically focus on a single objective or evaluate alternatives in limited settings. We address this gap by deriving a common formulation of objective-driven updates within a common Riemannian framework and comparing the resulting one-step generators across diverse settings. We call the resulting framework Riemannian Wasserstein Gradient Flows (R-WGF). We start from an explicit objective measuring the discrepancy between the model and target distributions. Its first variation describes how this objective changes, and the Riemannian metric converts this information into an intrinsic particle velocity. This velocity defines a continuous flow of the model distribution. Under explicit regularity assumptions, we show that the flow decreases the chosen objective. We then approximate the flow with geometry-compatible finite updates and, for the objectives considered, estimate these updates from samples and amortize them into a neural generator. Our contributions are: • We formulate objective-driven drifting through Riemannian Wasserstein calculus, making explicit how a law-level functional and a ground metric determine the particle velocity. • Under explicit regularity assumptions, we establish the population energy-dissipation identity. We also provide geometry-compatible finite updates through Riemannian retractions and prove their local first-order consistency with the exponential map. • We apply our Riemannian Wasserstein gradient-flow framework to three distinct domains, demonstrating one-step generation on spherical geospatial data, Binary-MNIST and discretized CIFAR-10 images, and LM1B text.

Our goal is to learn a generative model whose output distribution q q approximates the target p p while retaining fast sampling. Motivated by promising recent results in WGF-based generative modeling ( Gretton et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) , we follow this paradigm by decreasing ℱ p ​ ( q ) \mathcal{F}_{p}(q) . Third, we instantiate ℱ p \mathcal{F}_{p} with concrete objectives and derive the corresponding intrinsic drifts. Fourth, we replace the ideal flow by geometry-compatible finite steps and amortize those steps into a generator. The construction is independent of a particular ground geometry. Detailed Euclidean, spherical, and categorical realizations are collected in Appendix A .

3.4 Practical discretization and neural amortization
sections.text: The framework above describes how to move samples toward a target distribution. Our goal, however, is to train a model that can generate from that distribution in a single forward pass. We make this practical by discretizing the flow, estimating the drifting field with finite number of samples and amortizing its updates into a neural generator.

sections.heading: Relation to Drifting Models.
sections.text: Drifting Models regress ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) onto ϕ ⁡ ( x ) + V ⁡ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ) \phi(x)+V(\phi(x)) , so both the drift and the target live in feature space. In R-WGF, the feature map only defines which samples are close, while the metric 𝗀 \mathsf{g} defines how x x moves. The drift is pulled back to ℳ \mathcal{M} , and the target stays on ℳ \mathcal{M} .

sections.heading: Wasserstein gradient flows and drifting models.
sections.text: Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) regress a one-step generator onto samples displaced by a heuristic attraction–repulsion field. Later analyses showed that this field is a difference of smoothed scores only for Gaussian kernels ( Turan et al., 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Franz et al., 2026 ) , and that the practical algorithm is not the gradient flow of any functional ( Gretton et al., 2026 ) . Gretton et al. (2026) make the objective-first alternative explicit: the velocity is the negative gradient of the first variation of a chosen functional. This route has been followed with KDE-approximated divergences ( Cao et al., 2026 ) and with the Sinkhorn divergence ( Feydy et al., 2019 ) in Sinkhorn-Drifting ( He et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow scales it with a two-batch estimate of the self-term, which we also adopt. Drifting has further been used to refine discrete diffusion language models ( Oba et al., 2026 ) . All these methods are Euclidean: velocities live in an ambient or feature space and are applied additively. R-WGF keeps the objective-first recipe but makes the velocity, the update step, and the loss intrinsic to the manifold, and it recovers the fields above in the Euclidean case (Table 1 ).

sections.heading: Generation on Riemannian and categorical spaces.
sections.text: Generative models on manifolds regress intrinsic tangent fields along a prescribed probability path ( Chen and Lipman, 2024 ) . For categorical data, the Fisher–Rao geometry of the simplex underlies Fisher and statistical flow matching ( Davis et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) , alongside Dirichlet and discrete flow matching ( Stark et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) . One- and few-step variants learn flow maps of such paths, both on manifolds ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Davis et al., 2025 ; Woo et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) and for categorical data ( Roos et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , or build on learned or closed-form data–noise couplings ( Peng et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . Unlike these methods, R-WGF uses the geometry as the ground metric of a WGF ( Ambrosio et al., 2005 ; Erbar, 2010 ) , and its velocity comes from a distributional objective without a path or a time variable.

sections.heading: Geometry-aware drifting and the position of R-WGF.
sections.text: Three works are closest to ours. KGDM ( Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) replaces the Euclidean displacement in the drifting field by the kernel gradient grad 𝗀 , x ⁡ κ ρ ​ ( x , y ) \operatorname{grad}_{\mathsf{g},x}\kappa_{\rho}(x,y) . With the Parzen estimates p ^ ρ \widehat{p}_{\rho} and q ^ ρ \widehat{q}_{\rho} of Eq. ( 16 ), its drift is grad 𝗀 ⁡ log ⁡ p ^ ρ − grad 𝗀 ⁡ log ⁡ q ^ ρ \operatorname{grad}_{\mathsf{g}}\log\widehat{p}_{\rho}-\operatorname{grad}_{\mathsf{g}}\log\widehat{q}_{\rho} , which is exactly the KL branch of R-WGF. KGDM proves that this drift decreases a smoothed KL only in Euclidean space. Proposition 3.2 shows that the exact population flow dissipates on ℳ \mathcal{M} . Cao et al. (2026) outline a spherical variant with a von Mises–Fisher kernel. Since ‖ x − y ‖ 2 2 = 2 − 2 ​ x ⊤ ​ y \|x-y\|_{2}^{2}=2-2x^{\top}y on 𝕊 D − 1 \mathbb{S}^{D-1} , it coincides with our chordal-Gaussian KL field, but they do not specify how outputs stay on the manifold and show only a two-dimensional example. CatDrift ( Eijkelboom et al., 2026 ) uses a negative-entropy mirror update on the simplex, which has the same softmax form as our exponentiated retraction. By Propositions A.1 and 3.3 , this mirror step is a valid retraction and matches the exponential-map step up to O ⁡ ( η 2 ) O(\eta^{2}) . R-WGF differs from these works in three ways. First, it starts from the objective rather than the kernel. Any functional with a regular first variation and any ground metric give the drift V p , q = − grad 𝗀 ⁡ ψ p , q V_{p,q}=-\operatorname{grad}_{\mathsf{g}}\psi_{p,q} . Second, it yields Sinkhorn and MMD drifts on the sphere and on Fisher–Rao simplices, which, to our knowledge, have not been derived or evaluated before. The Riemannian Sinkhorn drift generalizes the Euclidean target-minus-self field ( He et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Third, it compares MMD, Sinkhorn, and KL under one protocol on spherical, image, and language data. Further related work is discussed in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate our method in three settings. First, following KGDM ( Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) , we model geospatial data intrinsically on 𝕊 2 \mathbb{S}^{2} . Second, following PairFlow ( Park et al., 2026 ) , we model binarized MNIST and discretized CIFAR-10 on a product simplices. Third, we extend the same product-simplex formulation to LM1B language modeling, building on FMLM ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . Full protocols and extended results are in Appendix B . The KL, MMD, and Sinkhorn variants of R-WGF are denoted R-WGF-KL, R-WGF-MMD, and R-WGF-Sinkhorn, respectively.

sections.heading: 5.1 Geospatial data on the sphere

For a fair comparison, we reproduce KGDM in our training pipeline. Theoretically, KGDM and R-WGF-KL are equivalent. In practice, we implemented one variant of KGDM model with a Laplace kernel, whereas our R-WGF-KL uses a Gaussian kernel. Section 4 discusses this relation. sections.heading: 5.3 Language modeling
sections.text: Following the FMLM setup ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate our method on LM1B ( Chelba et al., 2013 ) . Due to computational resource constraints, we initialize from the released pretrained FLM checkpoint and fine-tune it with the R-WGF objective rather than training from scratch. We split model development into two stages. Stage 1 uses a limited number of training iterations to compare tuned R-WGF-Sinkhorn and R-WGF-KL schedules. Sinkhorn achieves lower GenPPL (Appendix Fig. 6 ), so Stage 2 continues only R-WGF-Sinkhorn. We also tested R-WGF-MMD on LM1B in preliminary runs, but it was not competitive, so we omit it from this screening. Table 4 reports the final one-step results. R-WGF-Sinkhorn reaches 122.54 GenPPL with 4.16 entropy. It is thus competitive with FMLM (119.34 and 4.16) and substantially better than CFM. DFM (PSD) attains a lower GenPPL of 94.08, but its lower entropy of 4.06 indicates a partial collapse to less diverse text, which also lowers GenPPL. Full details are in Appendix B.4 . sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced R-WGF, a framework that extends objective-driven Wasserstein gradient-flow training to Riemannian state spaces. Under the stated assumptions, it yields intrinsic particle updates with objective dissipation and locally consistent finite steps, then amortizes the flow into a one-step generator. Experiments on 𝕊 2 \mathbb{S}^{2} and products of simplices show competitive results on geospatial data, Binary-MNIST, discretized CIFAR-10 images, and LM1B. Overall, respecting data geometry provides a practical route to fast generation beyond Euclidean spaces. Limitations are discussed in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Training lineage and checkpoint selection.
sections.text: The reported Sinkhorn model continues a 26,000-step Hellinger-only run: hard data and the hybrid MAE cost are introduced together, and the EMA checkpoint at global step 36,000 is retained. The KL model continues a 38,000-step Hellinger-kernel score run, adds the MAE term, and retains step 42,000. These two results are therefore continuations rather than from-scratch ablations of the final objective. R-WGF-MMD is trained from scratch for 50,000 updates and selects step 40,000.

sections.heading: FID protocol.
sections.text: We follow the PairFlow-compatible protocol ( Park et al., 2026 ) : argmax decode 1,000 EMA samples and compare them with all 60,000 Binary-MNIST training images. After checkpoint selection, each fixed checkpoint is evaluated on nine new sampling seeds. Consequently, the standard deviations in Table 3 measure sampling variability for one trained checkpoint, not variability across training runs.

sections.heading: Representation and generator.
sections.text: An image is represented as x ∈ ( Δ 255 ) 3072 x\in(\Delta^{255})^{3072} : one distribution over 256 intensities for each of the 32 × 32 × 3 32\times 32\times 3 subpixels of discretized CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . The generator is a U-Net with 128 base channels, channel multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 ) (1,2,2,2) , two residual blocks per scale, one attention resolution, and dropout 0.1 0.1 . It maps Gaussian noise of image shape to a truncated discretized logistic distribution for every subpixel ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , whose scale is bounded to [ 0.5 , 8 ] [0.5,8] intensity bins.

sections.heading: Objective.
sections.text: We use R-WGF-Sinkhorn with the covector retraction Eq. ( 26 ) and the multi-feature loss Eq. ( 20 ) with equal weights, η = 10 − 5 \eta=10^{-5} , and hard data targets. As for Binary-MNIST, d ℳ 2 d_{\mathcal{M}}^{2} is the sum of sitewise squared-Hellinger distances. The feature maps are the Hellinger coordinates on the product simplex, the expected RGB image and its channel RMS, and multi-layer features of a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) applied to the expected RGB image upsampled to 224 × 224 224\times 224 . For each live batch, we draw a data batch and an independent, detached model batch. Sinkhorn is solved on blocks of 64 × 64 64\times 64 particles per GPU, with the squared Euclidean feature cost divided by its batch scale and ε OT = 0.05 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{OT}}=0.05 in these units. The solver runs at most ten iterations in FP64 with tolerance 10 − 5 10^{-5} . Each drift is normalized by its Fisher–Rao RMS over the microbatch, as in Eq. ( 20 ).

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: We use Adam with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , no weight decay, 5,000 warmup updates and a constant schedule afterwards, gradient clipping at one, bfloat16 precision, and EMA decay 0.9999 0.9999 . The global batch is 8,192 images, with 64 images per GPU and gradient accumulation.

sections.heading: FID protocol.
sections.text: About every 500 updates, we draw 5,000 EMA samples with one NFE and argmax decoding. FID is computed against the statistics of the CIFAR-10 training set with the PairFlow implementation, and we retain the checkpoint with the lowest FID. We then evaluate this checkpoint on five new sampling seeds, with 5,000 and with 50,000 samples, and report the mean and standard deviation.

sections.text: This appendix complements Section 4 with a detailed comparison to inverse distillation and a broader overview of accelerated categorical generation.

sections.heading: Inverse distillation and IDLM.
sections.text: Inverse distillation transfers iterative generation from a pretrained teacher into the training of a few- or one-step generator. IBMD learns a generator-induced endpoint coupling whose bridge-matching solution reproduces a given bridge model ( Gushchin et al., 2025 ) , RealUID extends this idea to diffusion, flow, bridge, and stochastic-interpolant models with real-data supervision ( Kornilov et al., 2026 ) , and Residual Shifting Distillation applies it to one-step super-resolution ( Selikhanovych et al., 2026 ) . Its categorical instance, IDLM ( Li et al., 2026 ) , is the variant most closely related to our work. IDLM is the closest categorical precursor because it also optimizes an explicit functional of the current generator law and uses simplex-valued relaxations. Under its ideal population assumptions, its inverse-distillation functional is a model-to-target reverse KL between diffusion path measures and bounds the endpoint reverse KL. Using our endpoint notation ( q θ , p ) (q_{\theta},p) , and writing x = softmax ⁡ ( ℓ ) x=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell) and teacher–fake advantage a t = log ⁡ f ⋆ ​ ( u t , t ) − log ⁡ f ⁡ ( u t , t ) a_{t}=\log f^{\star}(u_{t},t)-\log f(u_{t},t) , its local logit gradient contains the same centered-simplex operator as the Fisher–Rao cometric: ℒ IDLM \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IDLM}} = ℒ ( f ⋆ , q θ ) − min f ℒ ( f , q θ ) = KL ( ℙ θ ∥ ℙ ⋆ ) ≥ KL ( q θ ∥ p ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(f^{\star},q_{\theta})-\min_{f}\mathcal{L}(f,q_{\theta})=\operatorname{KL}(\mathbb{P}_{\theta}\|\mathbb{P}^{\star})\geq\operatorname{KL}(q_{\theta}\|p), ∂ ℒ IDLM − MDLM ∂ ℓ i \displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IDLM-MDLM}}}{\partial\ell_{i}} = − λ t ​ x i ​ ( ( a t ) i − ⟨ x , a t ⟩ ) = − λ t ​ [ G FR ​ ( x ) ​ a t ] i , G FR ​ ( x ) = Diag ⁡ ( x ) − x ​ x ⊤ . \displaystyle=-\lambda_{t}x_{i}\bigl((a_{t})_{i}-\langle x,a_{t}\rangle\bigr)=-\lambda_{t}[G_{\mathrm{FR}}(x)a_{t}]_{i},\qquad G_{\mathrm{FR}}(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(x)-xx^{\top}. (33) Thus IDLM and R-WGF share an explicit law-level objective, reverse-KL orientation, shared-latent simplex outputs, and an algebraically identical centering operator ( Li et al., 2026 ) . The interpretation differs: IDLM backpropagates a frozen teacher–fake advantage through generator logits, whereas R-WGF maps an endpoint-law first variation through a chosen Fisher–Rao cometric to an intrinsic particle velocity and then amortizes that transport. Our MMD and Sinkhorn fields also require no diffusion teacher. Our executable KL branch instead uses a Parzen score approximation. The methods are therefore closely related, but neither is a special case of the other.

sections.heading: Accelerated categorical generation.
sections.text: Discrete, Dirichlet, Fisher, and statistical-manifold flow matching provide other routes to categorical generation ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Stark et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) . Recent work obtains one- or few-evaluation generation using learned flow maps, direct latent–data couplings, and diffusion–autoregressive refinement ( Roos et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . Dual-Stream Decoding instead accelerates a frozen autoregressive model at inference through parallel proposal and refinement ( Abulkhanov et al., 2026 ) . Our claim is therefore not priority for one-step categorical generation, but an objective-derived Fisher–Rao WGF on product simplices.

sections.heading: Experimental scale.
sections.text: Our empirical scope is limited by the available compute. The Earth benchmark and Binary-MNIST are relatively small. On discretized CIFAR-10, we evaluate only 32 × 32 32\times 32 images. The language study is restricted to LM1B, length-128 sequences, and a single 139M-parameter generator initialized from a released FLM checkpoint. We therefore do not establish scaling to high-resolution images, longer contexts, larger backbones, or additional language domains.

sections.heading: Population theory versus the training algorithm.
sections.text: The dissipation result applies to an exact, sufficiently smooth population flow under the stated chain-rule and boundary assumptions. It does not prove descent after every finite empirical update, convergence of stochastic neural optimization, or exact recovery of the target law by the amortized generator. The retraction guarantee is also local and first-order, so finite step sizes introduce discretization error. We further leave well-posedness, convergence rates, and global convergence of the population flow to future work.

sections.heading: Finite-sample and boundary approximations.
sections.text: MMD and Sinkhorn use empirical plug-in fields, and truncated Sinkhorn solves add numerical error. The practical KL branch instead estimates a Parzen-smoothed score field. In addition, the Fisher–Rao analysis is stated on compact subsets of the open simplex, whereas categorical observations lie on its boundary. The clipped projected updates used for Binary-MNIST and LM1B are practical boundary extensions and are not covered by the compact-interior guarantees. Discretized CIFAR-10 instead uses the exponentiated retraction, but its hard one-hot data also lie on the boundary. We also do not prove that improving a relaxed-space objective must improve metrics after argmax decoding.

However, existing formulations have been developed largely for continuous Euclidean domains, such as image spaces, where particles admit unconstrained additive updates. On constrained spaces, these updates can leave the valid domain or ignore its geometry, making them unsuitable targets for training. Recent work has adapted updates to these spaces, but has focused on particular fields or offered limited empirical comparison. We derive and compare several geometry-aware fields within a common training framework for one-step generators. We test the method on data with different structures and obtain competitive one-step results in each setting. The best-performing field varies by task, showing why the choice of objective matters in practice. Figure 1: Fixed- z z generation on a product of simplices. This transport is often realized through many sequential updates, making inference expensive. Drifting Models offer a complementary strategy: they update the model distribution iteratively during training and amortize the resulting moves into a generator that can be evaluated directly at inference time ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . Recent works connect such updates to Wasserstein gradient flows (WGFs), making it possible to derive the drift from an explicit objective ( Gretton et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Most such formulations, however, rely on Euclidean velocities and additive updates. Many data types and representations live naturally on curved or constrained spaces, where Euclidean updates need not follow the intrinsic geometry or even remain in the state space. Classical WGF theory extends beyond Euclidean spaces ( Ambrosio et al., 2005 ; Erbar, 2010 ) , and recent generative and drifting methods construct dynamics on Riemannian manifolds ( Chen and Lipman, 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) . However, they typically focus on a single objective or evaluate alternatives in limited settings. We address this gap by deriving a common formulation of objective-driven updates within a common Riemannian framework and comparing the resulting one-step generators across diverse settings. We call the resulting framework Riemannian Wasserstein Gradient Flows (R-WGF). We start from an explicit objective measuring the discrepancy between the model and target distributions. Its first variation describes how this objective changes, and the Riemannian metric converts this information into an intrinsic particle velocity. This velocity defines a continuous flow of the model distribution. Under explicit regularity assumptions, we show that the flow decreases the chosen objective. We then approximate the flow with geometry-compatible finite updates and, for the objectives considered, estimate these updates from samples and amortize them into a neural generator. Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) regress a one-step generator onto samples displaced by a heuristic attraction–repulsion field. Later analyses showed that this field is a difference of smoothed scores only for Gaussian kernels ( Turan et al., 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Franz et al., 2026 ) , and that the practical algorithm is not the gradient flow of any functional ( Gretton et al., 2026 ) . Gretton et al. (2026) make the objective-first alternative explicit: the velocity is the negative gradient of the first variation of a chosen functional. This route has been followed with KDE-approximated divergences ( Cao et al., 2026 ) and with the Sinkhorn divergence ( Feydy et al., 2019 ) in Sinkhorn-Drifting ( He et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow scales it with a two-batch estimate of the self-term, which we also adopt. Drifting has further been used to refine discrete diffusion language models ( Oba et al., 2026 ) . All these methods are Euclidean: velocities live in an ambient or feature space and are applied additively. R-WGF keeps the objective-first recipe but makes the velocity, the update step, and the loss intrinsic to the manifold, and it recovers the fields above in the Euclidean case (Table 1 ). Generation on Riemannian and categorical spaces. Generative models on manifolds regress intrinsic tangent fields along a prescribed probability path ( Chen and Lipman, 2024 ) . For categorical data, the Fisher–Rao geometry of the simplex underlies Fisher and statistical flow matching ( Davis et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) , alongside Dirichlet and discrete flow matching ( Stark et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) . One- and few-step variants learn flow maps of such paths, both on manifolds ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Davis et al., 2025 ; Woo et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) and for categorical data ( Roos et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , or build on learned or closed-form data–noise couplings ( Peng et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . Unlike these methods, R-WGF uses the geometry as the ground metric of a WGF ( Ambrosio et al., 2005 ; Erbar, 2010 ) , and its velocity comes from a distributional objective without a path or a time variable.
